awd_titl_txt: Conference: Actions on graphs and metric spaces
awd_abstract_narration:
This award will support U.S.-based students and early-career researchers to participate the workshop entitled “Actions on graphs and metric spaces” as part of the “Operators, graphs, groups” program at the Isaac Newton Institute of the University of Cambridge from September 1 through September 5, 2025. The workshop will focus on the study of groups, which are collections of transformations of objects that preserve certain geometric properties. The workshop will bring together leading experts to share recent advancements and explore new research directions. The interdisciplinary nature of the workshop, combined with the broader thematic semester, will facilitate communication among U.S. students and leading experts across multiple mathematical fields and enhance STEM education at the undergraduate and graduate levels.
 
The topic of the workshop is studying groups via their actions on graphs and metric spaces that satisfy various notions of non-positive curvature, such as the CAT(0) condition introduced by Alexandrov and the hyperbolicity condition defined by Gromov. Such a strategy has been successfully employed to study fundamental groups of 3-manifolds, as well as to explore the possible complexity of groups, leading to the resolution of the celebrated Virtual Haken Conjecture and the Day–von Neumann Conjecture. For more information, please visit https://www.newton.ac.uk/event/oggw02/.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
During the award period, this grant supported U.S. participation in the international workshop “Actions on Graphs and Metric Spaces,” held September 1–5, 2025, at the Isaac Newton Institute for Mathematical Sciences in Cambridge, United Kingdom. The workshop brought together speakers and researchers from North America, Europe, and Asia to study a central idea in modern mathematics: abstract symmetries can often be understood through the ways they move points in a geometric space. A graph can be pictured as a network of vertices and edges, while a metric space is any setting in which distance can be measured. Studying how groups of symmetries act on these spaces turns difficult algebraic questions into geometric questions that can often be visualized and compared.

Intellectual merit. The workshop connected several active areas of geometry, topology, and group theory. It featured 17 research lectures and substantial time for informal discussion. Topics included spaces with tree-like large-scale geometry, negatively curved spaces, nonpositively curved cube complexes, surface groups, Artin groups, growth, rigidity, algorithms, and dynamical questions. Participants presented recent advances, compared methods developed in different subfields, and discussed common open problems and promising research directions. A recurring theme was that techniques first created for one class of spaces can often be adapted to another. These exchanges clarified relationships among current theories, spread new tools rapidly, and helped participants develop or strengthen collaborations. The meeting also highlighted the influential contributions of mathematician Misha Kapovich to the field.

Broader impacts. NSF support reduced financial barriers to U.S. participation in a major international research meeting. The workshop created valuable opportunities for graduate students, postdoctoral scholars, and other early-career researchers to learn directly from established experts, refine ideas through discussion, build professional networks, and identify potential mentors and collaborators. The international range of the program strengthened connections between the U.S. mathematical community and researchers and institutions abroad. Scheduled breaks, shared meals, and open discussion periods provided sustained time for collaborative work that is difficult to obtain through ordinary short academic visits.

The project’s reach extended beyond those who could attend in person. Virtual participation was offered without charge, and 17 recorded lectures were made publicly available online. These recordings form a lasting educational resource for researchers, graduate students, seminar groups, and instructors. They allow the ideas and methods presented at the workshop to reach a wider audience and remain useful well beyond the award period.

As appropriate for a conference award, the principal outcomes were the rapid exchange of new knowledge, the formation and strengthening of research connections, the training and mentoring of emerging researchers, and the creation of a durable public record of current work. Together, these outcomes advanced foundational mathematics and helped build a more connected and accessible research community.
